chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, and Muhammad ibn Ismail, from Al-Fadl ibn Shazan, altogether from Ibn Abi Umayr, from Abd al-Rahman ibn al-Hajjaj, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said:

He (peace be upon him) asked me: 'Does Ibn Abi Layth judge with a judgment and then retract from it?' So I said to him: 'It has reached me that he judged regarding the chattels of the man and the woman when one of them died, so the heirs of the living and the heirs of the deceased claimed it, or the man divorced her, so the man claimed it and the women claimed it. He judged with four judgments.'

So he (peace be upon him) said: 'And what was that?' So I said: 'As for the first of them, he judged in it by the saying of Ibrahim al-Nakhai': he made the chattels of the woman which were not suitable for men to be for the woman, and the chattels of the man which were not suitable for women to be for the man, and whatever was for men and women, he divided it between them in two halves.'

Then it reached me that he said: 'They are both claimants together, so that which is in their hands entirely, he divided between them in two halves.' Then he said: 'The man is the owner of the house, and the woman is the one entering upon him, and she is the claimant, so all the chattels are for the man except the chattels of the women which do not belong to men, so these are for the woman.'

Then he judged after that with a judgment, had I not witnessed it, I would not have referred it to him. A woman from us died, and she had a husband, and she left chattels. So we raised the matter to him, so he said: 'Write down the chattels.' So when he read it, he said to the husband: 'This which is for the man and the woman, we have made it for the woman, except for the scale, for it is from the chattels of the man, so it is for you.'

So he (peace be upon him) said to me: 'So upon what is he today?' I said: 'He has reverted to what was said by the saying of Ibrahim al-Nakhai': that he made the house for the man.' Then I asked him about that, so I said to him: 'What do you say about it?' So he said: 'The saying which you informed me that you witnessed, even though he had reverted from it.'

So I said: 'The chattels are for the woman?' So he said: 'What is your view if she establishes proof, how much would she need?' I said: 'Two witnesses.' So he said: 'If you were to ask the ones between the two mountains, and we are at that time in Makkah, they would tell you that the dowry and the chattels are gifted openly from the house of the woman to the house of her husband, so she is the one who brought it. And this claimant, if he claims that he has added anything to it, let him bring proof upon it.'
ai.seo_question: How did the judge Ibn Abi Layth rule on the division of household property between husband and wife according to this hadith?
ai.summary: This hadith from *Al-Kafi* (Chapter 27) documents the jurisprudential evolution of the judge Ibn Abi Layth regarding household chattels (*matā'*), reflecting the dynamic nature of *fiqh* through his shifting rulings. It highlights the Shia scholarly emphasis on contextual evidence, particularly the custom of wives openly gifting items to the marital home, which shifts the burden of proof to the husband if he claims ownership of specific additions. This narrative underscores the practical application of legal reasoning (*ijtihad*) within the early Shia community in Mecca.
